# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems work. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62 pounds, and every foot of elevation you want to lift it costs you energy. When you turn on a faucet on the 30th floor of an apartment building, you're asking the city to deliver water roughly 300 feet above the street—and the system accomplishes this through a carefully engineered interplay of gravity, pressure, pumps, and storage. Let's trace how this happens, using a concrete example.

## The Driving Force: Elevation as Energy

Imagine a city with its main reservoir sitting on a hill 250 feet above the downtown area. The water utility doesn't primarily use pumps to push water to most customers—gravity does the work. Water stored at elevation possesses potential energy, and when it flows downhill through the distribution network, that elevation converts into pressure. Engineers measure this as "head": every 2.31 feet of elevation produces roughly 1 pound per square inch (psi) of pressure.
